sections.h2: How does a Texas property go to a tax sale?
sections.html:
Each year's taxes are secured by a lien that arises on the first day of January, and a bill left unpaid can end in a suit and then an auction of the property. The sale is a tax foreclosure auction, and the winning bidder receives a deed afterward.

The ladder runs in order: delinquency notices, an optional installment plan, then a suit by the taxing unit, with court costs added to the bill. Once a bill goes delinquent the Comptroller says the cost climbs: an initial penalty and interest charge is added, the penalty grows each month until July, and interest has no ceiling. Collection attorneys hired by the unit can add a further charge.

sections.h2: Who runs the sale and where is it held?
sections.html:
Tax foreclosure sales are auctions, typically run by the constable or an agent the taxing unit hires.

The State Law Library tells buyers and owners to check the county clerk or county tax office websites for sale notices. Because each taxing unit and county handles notices its own way, call the tax office that bills the property instead of trusting a general list. The lien survives a change of ownership, so a buyer at an ordinary sale who skips the tax check can end up with the liability.

sections.h2: Can the former owner get the property back after a Texas tax sale?
sections.html:
Yes, in a limited window, and the cost depends on the kind of property. Tax Code Section 34.21 governs redemption, as a Texas Supreme Court opinion explains.

Redemption rules for land auctioned for taxes, as described by the Texas Supreme Court
Kind of propertyRedemption periodPremium
Homestead, agricultural or mineral interestTwo years after the buyer's deed is filed25 percent in the first year, 50 percent in the second
Other property180th day after the deed is filedNot over 25 percent

Source: Texas Supreme Court opinion on Tax Code Section 34.21.

On top of that the owner repays the winning bid, the deed recording fee and the back charges. The purchaser must itemize those costs within 10 days of a written request, so a redeeming owner should put the request on paper.

sections.h2: Who gets the money when a property sells for more than the taxes owed?
sections.html:
Money left over once the tax debt and costs are paid is called excess proceeds, and the former owner has two years from the sale to claim them. Sections 34.03 and 34.04 of the Tax Code govern the process, according to the State Law Library.

If you suspect money is waiting for you, contact the court that ordered the sale and the tax office. Keep proof of your ownership and your current mailing address with your claim. Heirs of a deceased owner should be ready to show how they inherited, since the claim follows the same ownership questions that arise in probate.

sections.h2: What should a buyer check before bidding at a tax sale?
sections.html:
A buyer should confirm what the deed will and will not do, because the redemption right can reopen the deal after the sale.

  • Find out from the tax office which units' taxes the sale covers.
  • Check whether the property is a homestead, farmland or has a mineral interest, since these have the longer redemption period.
  • Review the county records for other liens. The comptroller files state tax liens with the county clerk, who records them in the state tax lien book.
  • Plan for the possibility of an occupant. If someone is living there, expect to need a court case to get possession.

The county clerk is the county recorder, so the clerk's office is also where the deed will be recorded afterward.

sections.h2: How can an owner avoid a tax sale in Texas?
sections.html:
Pay before the delinquency date or work out a payment plan. Plans on delinquent bills can run as long as 36 months with some collectors, and a homestead owner is entitled to one.

Penalty and interest waivers exist for many cases, but they require quick payment and a written request, so ask the collector for the exact deadlines on your bill. Older or disabled homeowners can split delinquent tax into four installments, and veterans with a disability rating may qualify for an exemption. If you are behind and thinking of selling, a sale that pays the tax at closing ends the lien problem before a lawsuit begins.

sections.h2: Does a tax sale affect a seller trying to sell a house?
sections.html:
It does, because a buyer cannot get clear title until the delinquent taxes are paid. A seller with unpaid tax should get a payoff number from the title company and pay the tax from closing funds.

The January 1 owner owes that year's tax, and a suit can still reach that person after a sale. Get the paid-in-full records from the tax office after closing and keep them.

sections.h2: What does the Texas property tax calendar mean for a seller?
sections.html:
Values are fixed on January 1, bills are mailed near October 1, and a split payment lets an owner pay half in November and the balance in June.

Most owners need to pay by January 31, because taxes unpaid on February 1 are delinquent. Late-mailed bills get a later delinquency date. An owner who disagrees with the appraised value takes that dispute to the appraisal review board, generally by mid-May. After the board, an owner can appeal to district court, binding arbitration, or the state's administrative hearings office when the board value tops $1,000,000.

  • Section 23.23 caps yearly increases in a homestead's appraised value at 10 percent.
  • Section 11.26 can freeze school tax for an older or disabled homeowner.
  • An owner who appeals should still pay the amount not in dispute on time.

sections.h2: What help exists for owners who are behind on taxes?
sections.html:
Ask the county tax assessor-collector about installment plans, waivers and exemptions before a suit is filed. Many taxing units contract with the assessor-collector, so one office often handles the bill for several units.

The Comptroller notes that those homeowners can pay delinquent amounts in installments, with a 6 percent charge on the late installment and monthly interest. Disabled veterans should ask the appraisal district about the exemption that matches their VA rating.

sections.h2: What should an owner do after receiving a notice of tax suit or sale?
sections.html:
Act on it the same week. Call the tax office named on the notice, ask for the full payoff with court costs included, and ask whether the collector offers a payment plan for the delinquent years. Collection ladders in Texas move from notices to a plan to a lawsuit, and each step adds expense, so the cheapest moment to resolve a debt is the earliest one.

  • Write down the cause number and the court named on any suit papers.
  • Ask the clerk of that court how an excess proceeds claim would be filed.
  • Keep copies of every payment receipt, since the owner of record remains answerable for the year's tax.
  • If you plan to sell, give the title company the tax office's payoff letter right away.

Heirs and family members sometimes learn about a delinquent bill only after the owner has died. In that situation the first job is to sort out who holds title, because the person who can negotiate with the tax office is the owner or someone authorized to act for the estate.

faqs.q: Is there a redemption period after a Texas tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Homestead, farm and mineral property carries a two-year window. Other property gets roughly half a year.

faqs.q: What premium does a redeeming owner pay?
faqs.a: For the two-year category, the premium is 25 percent if the owner redeems in year one and 50 percent in year two. Other property carries a premium of no more than 25 percent.

faqs.q: When does the right to claim leftover sale money end?
faqs.a: Two years after the sale. Claims go through the court that ordered the sale under Tax Code Sections 34.03 and 34.04.

faqs.q: When do Texas property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: Usually on February 1 following the bill year, when penalty and interest start to run.

faqs.q: Where do I find tax sale listings?
faqs.a: No single statewide list exists. Check the county clerk and county tax office websites, or call the tax office that bills the property.
